entry.content:

entry.title: ICE and HSI Conduct Sweeping Surveillance Operation Targeting Left-Wing Groups
entry.content:
Links: wired.com | hacker news

Court documents from a federal conspiracy prosecution in Minnesota reveal that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) have conducted a sweeping domestic surveillance operation targeting left-wing activists, labor unions, and community response networks. Initiated under National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 and funded through programs like Operation Keyhole, the multi-agency campaign utilized undercover agents, drones, and invasive digital tools typically reserved for counterterrorism and international crime.

Defense attorneys and former law enforcement officials compare the directive to the FBI’s historic COINTELPRO operations, noting the vast scale of data collection involving intercepted encrypted chats, financial records, and commercial data brokers. The filings indicate that the surveillance extended far beyond Minnesota to activists and conferences in cities across the United States as part of a broader federal crackdown on opponents of the administration's immigration policies.

entry.title: Apple Developer Tools on macOS Still Trust Compromised eMudhra Certificates
entry.content:
Links: emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com | hacker news

Developer tools bundled with macOS—including git, curl, and python3—continue to trust compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates more than a week after Apple was notified of the security incident. Additionally, the recent release of macOS 27.2 failed to address the issue and overwrote manual workarounds applied by users, leaving development environments vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

This trust flaw allows attackers to intercept HTTPS connections, tamper with repository clones and pushes, and capture sensitive credentials like GitHub tokens. While Apple has secured Safari and applications using its core networking framework, developers must manually remove the affected root certificates and reapply fixes after system updates until an official patch is issued.

entry.title: Ghostty 1.4.0 Released With Complete Kitty Graphics Support and Performance Improvements
entry.content:

Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major update to the cross-platform terminal emulator that introduces a fully compliant Kitty graphics implementation supporting animation and relative placements, making it the first terminal outside of Kitty to achieve this. The release incorporates large-scale performance optimizations, memory reductions via scrollback compression, and a new EGL-based rendering pipeline for GTK.

Additional updates include expanded SSH integration, implementation of the Kitty clipboard protocol, split-pane dragging for GTK, and several security vulnerability patches. Performance enhancements yield higher end-to-end I/O throughput, faster text parsing, reduced CPU resource usage, and lower GPU resource consumption for hidden tabs.

entry.title: David Harvey Discusses Recently Proposed Sub-O(n log n) Integer Multiplication Algorithm
entry.content:
Links: web.maths.unsw.edu.au | hacker news

Mathematician David Harvey has published a commentary examining a recently proposed integer multiplication algorithm that claims a complexity of o(n log n) bit operations. The analysis offers perspective on the new complexity claim and its relation to established theoretical limits in computational mathematics.

The discussion follows earlier milestones in the field, including Harvey and Joris van der Hoeven's 2019 algorithm achieving O(n log n) bit operations, which confirmed a long-standing conjecture by Schönhage and Strassen. The newly proposed approach pushes past that established boundary into sub-O(n log n) territory, prompting careful scrutiny of its methods and assumptions.

entry.title: Ellia Lebleu Discusses Wikipedia's Ongoing Cleanup of AI-Generated Content
entry.content:
Links: spectrum.ieee.org | hacker news

In an interview with IEEE Spectrum, WikiProject AI Cleanup founding member Ellia Lebleu discusses the volunteer efforts launched in late 2023 to detect and remove artificial intelligence-generated material from Wikipedia. Lebleu notes that while early AI content was marked by glaring clichés and predictable structures, modern machine-generated submissions have become increasingly subtle, often featuring faulty citations and nuanced rhetorical patterns.

Despite the English Wikipedia's policy prohibiting large language models for content generation, volunteers estimate that AI text still accounts for a notable percentage of new drafts and submissions. The project relies on developing detection tools, automated verifiers, and coordination with the Wikimedia Foundation, raising broader questions about maintaining Wikipedia as a uniquely human-written corpus in an era dominated by generative AI.

Civil liberties groups and key legislators are demanding transparency regarding the court's findings before any debate on renewing the authority, which currently continues under interim court authorization after lapsing in June.

Full-stack engineer and tech executive Orestis Ioannou analyzes his GitHub contribution history to examine how adopting parallel AI coding agents significantly increased his workload rather than reducing it. Despite transitioning to leadership roles with less direct coding responsibility, utilizing multiple agents concurrently allowed him to pursue vastly more projects, returning his output to peak engineering levels.

The analysis highlights that low-cost implementation drives continuous cycles of intense coding bursts, context-switching fatigue, and burnout, while elevating baseline activity during quieter periods. Ioannou notes that while AI makes turning ideas into reality easier, human cognitive capacity for managing parallel workflows has not scaled at the same rate.

entry.title: Jan van den Berg Examines The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI
entry.content:
Links: j11g.com | hacker news

Software engineer Jan van den Berg reevaluates Frederick P. Brooks Jr.'s classic 1975 principle, Brooks's Law, to determine whether adding AI agents to a development project bypasses traditional scaling limits. While generative AI tools and LLMs eliminate human onboarding bottlenecks and coffee breaks, foundational software constraints persist.

Sequential tasks and the inherent limitations of dependency management remain unchanged, while overhead shifts from human coordination to agent orchestration. Deploying multiple autonomous agents without precise requirements and structured oversight only leads to conflicting code edits, proving that adding AI capacity to a flawed project accelerates failure.

entry.title: Python Experimental JIT Compiler to Be Removed From CPython Main
entry.content:
Links: lwn.net | source | discussion | hacker news

Python's experimental just-in-time compiler, introduced in CPython 3.13, is set to be removed from the main branch following the withdrawal of PEP 836. The Python steering council had previously paused JIT development in June, giving maintainers a six-month deadline to produce a standards-track proposal addressing maintenance commitments, compatibility, and security concerns.

Although the authors drafted PEP 836 in response, they ultimately withdrew the proposal after facing extensive steering council feedback and citing a lack of personal bandwidth. Consequently, development on the project has ended in the main repository, leaving its future entirely dependent on whether external contributors decide to pick it up elsewhere.
